title: Sullivan v. O’Connor
summary: A patient recovered for expenses, worsened appearance, and an additional operation after a promised cosmetic result failed. The parties’ appellate waivers limited the court’s need to choose between expectation and reliance measures.
notes:
Court: Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts (1973).

Sullivan was a professional entertainer, and the trial judge's instruction let the jury compensate her out-of-pocket expenses, the disfigurement, related emotional distress in light of her profession, and the pain and suffering of the third operation (363 Mass. 579, 296 N.E.2d 183, decided May 9, 1973).

sections.Parties: Alice Sullivan, a professional entertainer, sued plastic surgeon James O’Connor for negligence and breach of a promise to improve her nose and appearance.
sections.Material Facts:
O’Connor allegedly promised improvement through two operations. Those operations failed, and he performed a third. Sullivan remained disfigured, and further surgery could not improve the result. She paid a total of $622.65 in the physician’s fee and hospital expenses. Although O’Connor knew her profession, she did not prove lost employment resulting from her appearance.

The third operation mattered because it went beyond the two operations contemplated when she agreed to treatment. The case therefore permitted a distinction between burdens she expected to undergo even with successful performance and additional burdens caused by the unsuccessful outcome.
sections.Procedural History: The jury rejected negligence but awarded Sullivan $13,500 on the contract claim. O’Connor challenged instructions allowing recovery beyond out-of-pocket expenses. Sullivan had objected to the failure to award the whole difference between the promised and actual appearance, but waived that objection if the court rejected O’Connor’s appeal. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts overruled his exceptions; Sullivan’s exceptions were waived, leaving the verdict in place.
sections.Issue: Was recovery confined to money paid out, or could it include disfigurement and the pain and distress of the additional operation? Did resolving those objections require the court to choose a single general measure for all physician-promise cases?
sections.Holding: The challenged items were recoverable. Expenses, worsening of condition, and the additional operation’s pain and mental distress could be compensated on either an expectation or a reliance view in this posture. The waivers made a definitive choice between those views unnecessary.
sections.Reasoning:
Expectation compares actual performance with the promised result. Reliance compares the patient’s actual position with the position before undertaking treatment in reliance on the promise. Restitution concerns benefits transferred to the defendant. Sullivan’s claim could not be reduced to restitution merely because the surgeon was not negligent: a promise of a result can be breached without negligent conduct.

The court nevertheless saw reasons for caution about full expectation awards in this setting, including proof problems and the difficulty of assigning monetary value to an imagined successful appearance. It discussed the merits of a reliance measure without making that discussion a categorical rule resolving every medical-contract case. Mental and physical distress were sufficiently connected to the subject of the undertaking to be relevant here; broad statements excluding such damages from all contract actions were too sweeping.

The procedural limitation is decisive. Sullivan relinquished the disputed portions that would have forced a choice: ordinary pain of the first two operations and the value of promised improvement beyond her original condition. The court could uphold the remaining award without deciding which overall theory should govern those unclaimed elements.

priorVersions.summary: An unsuccessful promised nose improvement supported damages for expenses, worsening, and the additional operation; the preserved issues did not require a single exclusive choice between reliance and expectation.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts (1973).

The following problems vary operative pain, improvement, deterioration, expenses, and opportunities forgone. Keep an item’s place in a damages calculation separate from the legal basis for enforcing the promise.

sections.Parties: Sullivan, a professional entertainer, sued O’Connor, the surgeon who undertook to improve the appearance of her nose.
sections.Material Facts: The alleged agreement contemplated two operations and an improved appearance. Three operations left Sullivan worse off. Her out-of-pocket expenses were $622.65. The jury awarded $13,500 on the contract count and found for the surgeon on negligence.
sections.Procedural History: The surgeon challenged the inclusion of damages beyond expenses. Sullivan waived claims for the promised improvement and the pain of the first two operations. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts upheld the award on the issues preserved for review.
sections.Issue: Can the patient recover for deterioration and additional pain following breach of a promised surgical result, even though the surgeon was not negligent? What interests do those damages protect?
sections.Holding: The challenged recovery was permissible. Expenses, worsening of the patient’s condition, associated distress, and the pain of the third operation could be recovered in this setting. The court did not require Sullivan to receive only a refund.
sections.Reasoning: Negligence and breach of a contractual undertaking differ. The opinion discusses the possible harshness of full expectation awards in medical cases and the availability of reliance relief. On the posture presented, deterioration and the third operation’s pain are compatible with either approach. The original operative pain might figure in reliance but was waived; the value of the promised improvement would be an expectation component but was also waived. Reading the decision as selecting reliance for every medical-promise case would exceed what these preserved issues establish.

learning.why: Read the appellate objections before extracting a damages rule. The opinion explains three remedial interests, but the actual judgment rests on a narrower set of preserved claims.

topics.expectation: The promised improved appearance supplies one possible benchmark.
topics.reliance-damages: Restoration to the pre-treatment position supplies another.
topics.restitution: The court distinguishes fees received by the surgeon from the patient’s wider losses.
topics.certainty: Valuing an imagined successful appearance presents proof difficulties.
topics.promise-or-prediction: The opinion first asks whether a physician's statements about surgical results are enforceable promises or mere therapeutic reassurance, requiring clear proof before a doctor's prediction becomes a contract.
topics.reliance-interest: Sullivan is the standard case for measuring reliance damages (expenses, worsened condition, pain of the third operation) as an alternative to expectation.
